title: Quick reference: traffic control numbers
text: MUTCD taper formulas: 40 mph or less, L = W x S squared / 60; 45 mph or more, L = W x S (W = offset in ft, S = speed in mph). Merging taper L; shifting 1/2 L; shoulder 1/3 L; flagger one-lane two-way taper 50 to 100 ft; downstream taper 50 to 100 ft. 12 ft lane at 35 mph: 245 ft; at 55 mph: 660 ft. Advance sign spacing (national Table 6B-1; the road agency decides which streets are low or high speed, and some state manuals set it by mph): urban low speed 100 ft each; urban high speed 350 ft; rural 500 ft; freeway 1,000, 1,500, 2,640 ft. Buffer and flagger distance: 30 mph 200 ft; 35 mph 250 ft; 45 mph 360 ft; 55 mph 495 ft. Cone spacing guidance: taper, speed in mph as feet; tangent, twice that. Check your state standards and MUTCD edition.

title: Advance warning signs, flaggers and buffer space
text: Typical advance warning sign spacing (the MUTCD sign spacing table, distances A, B, C between signs): urban low speed 100 ft each (the road agency sets the speed category; some state manuals set it by mph); urban high speed 350 ft; rural 500 ft; expressway and freeway 1,000 / 1,500 / 2,640 ft. Leave a longitudinal buffer space ahead of the work when possible. Flaggers: trained (many states require flagger certification), wearing high-visibility apparel (ANSI 107 Class 2 or 3), using a STOP/SLOW paddle, standing on the shoulder next to the lane they control or in the closed lane, where approaching drivers can see them in time, with an escape route; give the flagger a flagger-ahead sign in advance. Nighttime work needs lighting and retroreflective gear. The permit's traffic control plan governs on that job.

title: Water main disinfection and bac-T samples (AWWA C651)
text: Keep pipe clean during laying, then disinfect before connecting to the system. AWWA C651 methods: continuous feed (water with at least 25 mg/L free chlorine fills the main, held 24 hours, ending with at least 10 mg/L), tablet (25 mg/L, 24 hours, water above 41 F), or slug (100 mg/L passed through for at least 3 hours). Agency specs can be stronger (Greenbook: 50 to 100 mg/L, 24 hours, 25 mg/L residual). Flush until the water is at system chlorine levels, dechlorinate the flush water before discharge, then take bacteriological (bac-T) samples: two sets that both pass, taken as the spec says (AWWA C651-14: a second set at least 16 hours after the first, or let the main sit 16 hours and take two sets 15 minutes apart; specs written on the 2005 edition say 24 hours apart), or per the agency; all must show no coliform. Don't connect until samples pass, and resample if the main isn't put in service in time.

title: Quick reference: water main test numbers
text: Common water main numbers (check your spec, which governs). Hydrostatic test: AWWA C600 per U.S. Pipe, at least 1.25 times working pressure at the high point and 1.5 times at the low point; some utilities use 150 psi or 1.5 times working pressure, others working pressure plus 100 psi; hold at least 2 hours. Allowable make-up water L (gallons per hour) = S x D x square root of P / 148,000; for 1,000 ft of 8 inch at 150 psi, about 0.66 gal/hr. Disinfection (AWWA C651): continuous feed at least 25 mg/L, held 24 hours, at least 10 mg/L remaining; slug at least 100 mg/L for 3 hours; tablet about 25 mg/L for 24 hours. Bac-T samples every 1,200 ft plus end and branches, two consecutive acceptable sets. Flush before chlorinating at 3.0 ft per second or more (AWWA C651-14 Sec. 4.4.2; the 2005 edition said 2.5 ft per second, which is about 390 gpm in 8 inch).
source: AWWA C600 (U.S. Pipe), utility specs, AWWA C651 summary

text: Federal OSHA requires a protective system (sloping, benching, shoring or a shield) in an excavation 5 ft or deeper unless it is entirely in stable rock, and in a shallower one when the competent person sees a cave-in hazard (29 CFR 1926.652). Twenty-one states run their own OSHA plan for private construction crews; a plan must be at least as protective as federal and may be stricter, so on those jobs cite the state rule. What has been checked against the state's own rule text so far (as of 2026-11-20): Washington requires protection at 4 ft and, since June 1, 2026, a written trench work plan and a competent person on site during trench work; California keeps 5 ft and adds a Cal/OSHA permit for excavations 5 ft or deeper that people enter; Michigan uses its own Part 9 (slope or support over 5 ft, with its own angle table); Arizona, Nevada, New Mexico, Oregon and Utah adopt the federal excavation standard, so 5 ft; Alaska, Kentucky, Minnesota and Tennessee adopt the federal rule and Hawaii, North Carolina and Virginia list no excavation rule of their own (from OSHA's and the agencies' pages, not each state code read line by line), so 5 ft; South Carolina uses the federal text and adds training to the competent person definition. Not yet checked: Indiana, Iowa, Maryland (a state supplement to the federal rule exists and was not read), Vermont and Wyoming; treat federal 5 ft as the floor there and ask the state agency or your safety person whether the plan adds anything. In every state the competent person and your company program decide what protection a trench gets.
title: State OSHA plans and trench protection depth: which rule book applies on your job
topic: State OSHA plans: where trench and confined space rules differ from federal OSHA
source: 29 CFR 1926.652(a)(1); osha.gov/stateplans; Wash. Admin. Code 296-155-657; 8 CCR 341; Mich. Admin. Code R 408.40941; AZ R20-5-601; UT R614-1-4; OR 437-003-0001; NM 11.5.3.9 NMAC; checked 2026-11-20

title: Table B-1 maximum allowable slopes (OSHA 1926 Subpart P Appendix B), in words
text: OSHA's Table B-1 (Appendix B to Subpart P) gives the steepest slope allowed for excavations less than 20 ft deep, as horizontal to vertical: stable rock, vertical (90 degrees); Type A, 3/4 to 1 (53 degrees); Type B, 1 to 1 (45 degrees); Type C, 1 1/2 to 1 (34 degrees). Footnote 2: a short-term slope of 1/2 to 1 (63 degrees) is allowed in Type A only for excavations 12 ft or less deep; short term means open 24 hours or less; a short-term Type A cut deeper than 12 ft goes back to 3/4 to 1. Footnote 3: sloping or benching deeper than 20 ft must be designed by a registered professional engineer; since the table covers only less than 20 ft, exactly 20 ft and deeper is engineer-designed (the app's Trench Sloping screen says the same). Lay-back per side = depth x ratio: a 10 ft Type C trench lays back 15 ft each side. When there are signs of distress (fissures, slumping, bulging or heaving at the bottom, spalling, ravelling), the slope must be cut back at least 1/2 horizontal to 1 vertical flatter than the table (Appendix B (c)(3)). The OSHA library chunk for Appendix B (c) carries Table B-1 as text; this chunk is a plain-language copy of the official table, and the competent person picks the system.
topic: OSHA excavation appendices in plain words: slopes, benches, shoring tables
source: 29 CFR 1926 Subpart P Appendix B, Table B-1 with footnotes 1-3 and paragraphs (b), (c)(3)

title: Figure B-1 benching rules in words: 4 ft first bench, Type A and B only
text: Appendix B Figure B-1 shows the only bench shapes OSHA allows without an engineer. Type A (cohesive, 1.5 tsf or more): simple bench or multiple benches with the overall profile inside 3/4 to 1; the bottom (first) bench is at most 4 ft high and benches above it at most 5 ft. Type B: single or multiple benches inside 1 to 1, each bench at most 4 ft, and only in cohesive Type B soil (no benching in granular Type B). Type C: no benching at all; slope it 1 1/2 to 1, shore it, or shield it. Benching from this figure is for excavations less than 20 ft deep; at 20 ft or deeper a registered professional engineer designs it. A bench cut taller than the figure allows, or a bench in Type C or in granular soil, is an unprotected vertical face. Because benching eats width (a 10 ft Type B trench needs 20 ft of lay-back plus the bottom), it is used in open ground, not streets. The competent person classifies the soil and picks the system; this is a word copy of a drawing, check the official figure.
topic: OSHA excavation appendices in plain words: slopes, benches, shoring tables
source: 29 CFR 1926 Subpart P Appendix B, Figure B-1 (bench dimensions as summarized in OSHA's Trenching and Excavation publication and OSHA-based training material)

title: Flagger basics
text: Flaggers stand on the shoulder next to the lane they control, or in the closed lane, and step into the open lane only after traffic has stopped (MUTCD flagger procedures); clearly visible well ahead, with an escape route, wearing high-visibility apparel (class 2 or 3), using a STOP/SLOW paddle (not a flag, except in emergencies). Signs warn ahead of the flagger ("Flagger Ahead" symbol). Flaggers must be trained and certified where the state requires it. Never turn your back on traffic, and coordinate with the flagger at the other end by radio or sight.
topic: Traffic control and work zones (MUTCD Part 6 concepts)
source: Standard industry practice (AWWA, ASTM, PPI, MUTCD, utility company standards as noted); written for The Pipelayer's Bible

title: Traffic next to the trench: vests, barriers and work zone rules (1926.651(d), MUTCD Part 6)
text: 1926.651(d): employees exposed to public vehicular traffic must be given and wear warning vests or other reflectorized or high-visibility garments (ANSI 107 Class 2 or 3 in practice). The traffic control plan (MUTCD Part 6, the California MUTCD, and the encroachment permit) sets the lane closure, tapers, buffer, flaggers and channelizers; the trench itself gets positive protection where traffic runs next to it (drums or barricades at least, barrier where the permit requires). Steel plates over open trenches in roadways at the end of the day: OSHA treats them as covers, which in a roadway must hold at least twice the maximum axle load of the largest vehicle expected to cross and be secured against moving (1926.502(i)); the road agency's encroachment permit sets the plate thickness by trench width, how far the plate laps past the edges, pinning and ramping. Never leave a trench open overnight with only cones. Pedestrian routes get a protected detour or a covered walkway.
topic: Trench crossings, walkways, loads, traffic and public protection (OSHA 1926.651, 1926.501/502)
source: 29 CFR 1926.651(d); FHWA MUTCD Part 6 and California MUTCD; Caltrans Encroachment Permits Manual section 602.1 (steel plate bridging); city encroachment permit conditions
